industries.name: Healthcare & Health Systems
industries.meta_title: Behavioral Science in Healthcare & Health Systems
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science in healthcare for health systems: improve adherence, patient experience and clinician wellbeing with predictive KPIs and tested design.
industries.summary: Behavioral science in healthcare for health systems that want better adherence, stronger patient experience, sustainable clinical teams and measurable progress on cardiac and chronic risk.
industries.lede: Behavioral science in healthcare starts with a simple observation: most outcomes depend on what patients and clinicians do between encounters. We help health systems read those behavioral signals, design better care experiences and measure what actually moves health.
context: Health systems are built around encounters, yet most of health happens between them. A patient leaves a cardiology visit with a new prescription, a referral to cardiac rehabilitation and a follow-up date. Whether any of it happens depends on motivation, ability and a well-timed prompt, not on the quality of the visit alone. Adherence gaps, missed referrals and readmissions are behavioral problems that show up in clinical and financial data long before anyone names them as behavior. Behavioral science in healthcare gives leaders a way to see those patterns and act on them.

Inside the organization, the people problems are just as real. Clinicians carry heavy documentation loads, fragmented workflows and constant interruption, and burnout erodes the empathy and attention that patient experience depends on. Service line leaders are asked to improve access, quality scores and margin at once, often with data spread across the electronic health record, scheduling, call centers, patient portals and survey vendors that were never designed to speak to one another. Decisions get made on assumptions because the integrated picture does not exist.

Current forces raise the stakes. Value-based contracts reward prevention and adherence rather than volume. Patients compare their care experience with the convenience of consumer services. Digital front doors, remote monitoring and AI documentation tools promise relief but succeed only when people actually adopt them. Cardiac risk reduction, diabetes management and other chronic conditions require months of sustained self-management. Each of these shifts turns patient and clinician behavior into a strategic variable that health systems need to measure, predict and design for.

challenges.title: Adherence that fades after discharge
challenges.body: Patients often leave with clear instructions and good intentions, then stop medications, skip cardiac rehabilitation or miss follow-up visits within weeks. The causes are rarely a lack of information. They include cost, side effects, competing demands and the absence of a timely prompt. Without behavioral data, care teams see the lapse only after it becomes a readmission.

challenges.title: Patient experience measured too late
challenges.body: Experience surveys arrive weeks after the encounter and describe how people felt, not what they did. Leaders struggle to link survey scores to behaviors that matter, such as portal use, appointment keeping and willingness to return. The result is improvement work aimed at the score rather than at the moments that shape trust and loyalty.

challenges.title: Clinician burnout and workflow friction
challenges.body: Burnout is often framed as an individual resilience problem when much of it is designed into workflows, inbox volume and handoffs. Clinicians who feel overloaded have less capacity for the conversations that drive adherence and satisfaction. Programs that focus only on wellness offerings, without changing the work itself, tend to disappoint both clinicians and leaders.

challenges.title: Data spread across disconnected systems
challenges.body: Clinical records, scheduling, contact centers, portals, pharmacy and survey platforms each hold a fragment of the patient journey. Few health systems have integrated them around the behaviors that predict outcomes. Analysts fill the gaps with assumptions, and leaders end up debating anecdotes instead of testing which moments in the journey actually change health and cost.

challenges.title: Digital tools that patients and staff do not adopt
challenges.body: Health systems invest in portals, remote monitoring, scheduling apps and AI documentation tools that see uneven use. Adoption stalls when tools add steps, arrive at the wrong moment or ask for trust that has not been earned. Treating adoption as a behavioral design problem, rather than a rollout task, changes what success looks like.

how_we_help.title: Adherence and risk reduction design
how_we_help.body: We map the post-visit journey for a target population, such as patients recovering from a cardiac event, and identify the moments where adherence breaks down. We then design prompts, simplified routines and care team scripts grounded in health behavior models, and test them in pilots that measure filled prescriptions, rehabilitation attendance and follow-up completion.

how_we_help.title: Predictive patient experience KPIs
how_we_help.body: Using Behavioral Signals Design, we connect survey, scheduling, portal and contact center data to find the behaviors that precede loyalty or attrition. We replace lagging satisfaction scores with predictive, behavior-based KPIs that service line leaders can act on weekly, and we build dashboards that show where to intervene before experience problems reach the survey.

how_we_help.title: Clinician wellbeing grounded in the work
how_we_help.body: We study clinician workflows through observation and interviews, identify the friction points that drain time and attention, and co-design changes with the people who do the work. Paired with leadership and team coaching, this approach treats burnout as a systems problem and measures progress through behavior, retention signals and validated wellbeing instruments.

how_we_help.title: Patient journey and service design
how_we_help.body: We map the full patient journey across access, visit, discharge and follow-up, including the hidden handoffs between departments. Service design then addresses the moments that cause confusion or drop-off, from referral scheduling to discharge instructions, so that the experience patients have matches the care the organization intends to deliver.

how_we_help.title: Evidence-based health communication
how_we_help.body: Many patient messages are accurate but hard to act on. We rewrite and test outreach, discharge materials and portal messages using behavioral science and plain-language principles, then measure response through controlled comparisons. The goal is communication that respects patient autonomy and makes the next healthy step easier to take.

industries.impact_lens: Health systems exist to help people live longer, healthier lives, and much of that mission depends on behavior outside the clinic walls. Behavioral science advances it by making the healthy choice easier, better timed and more personally meaningful, especially for patients managing cardiac risk or chronic conditions. It also protects the people who provide care by redesigning the work that drives burnout. Done ethically, this approach supports patient autonomy rather than overriding it, and it directs scarce clinical attention to the moments where it can do the most good for patients and communities.

faqs.q: How is behavioral science in healthcare different from traditional patient engagement?
faqs.a: Traditional engagement programs often focus on delivering information or reminders. Behavioral science in healthcare starts by asking what specific behavior needs to happen, then examines motivation, ability and prompts for that behavior in a real patient population. Interventions are designed for the moments that matter and tested against measurable outcomes, so health systems learn what works rather than assuming that more outreach produces better adherence.

faqs.q: Can you work with our existing EHR and analytics data?
faqs.a: Yes. Most engagements begin with the data a health system already has, including clinical, scheduling, portal, contact center and survey sources. We identify the behavioral signals within those systems, note where gaps are being filled by assumptions and recommend practical ways to connect sources. We work alongside internal analytics and IT teams and do not require a new platform to begin.

faqs.q: Do you address clinician burnout as well as patient behavior?
faqs.a: Yes. Clinician wellbeing and patient outcomes are closely linked, so we treat both as part of the same system. Our work on burnout combines workflow research, co-design with clinicians and leadership coaching. We focus on changing the conditions of the work, such as handoffs and inbox design, rather than relying solely on individual resilience programs.

industries.name: Venture-Backed Startups
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science for venture-backed startups: founder coaching, scaling teams, activation signals and predictive KPIs that founders and investors trust.
industries.summary: Behavioral science for venture-backed startups and their investors: founder-led leadership, scaling teams, product activation signals and predictive KPIs for board and investor reporting.
industries.lede: Venture-backed startups grow by learning faster than their resources run out. We help founders and their investors find the behavioral signals that predict traction, build leadership teams that scale and report KPIs that show progress early.
context: Founders of venture-backed startups make high-stakes decisions with limited data. Early traction can be noisy: a handful of enthusiastic customers, a spike from a launch or growth driven by the founder's personal selling. The questions that matter most are behavioral. Which users reach real value, which behaviors predict retention and which customers will expand? Answering them early, from small and messy datasets, determines whether a team builds on solid ground or scales an assumption that has not been tested.

Founder-led leadership is both a strength and a constraint. Founders hold the vision, the customer relationships and many of the decisions. As teams grow from a few people to dozens or hundreds, the habits that worked early, such as deciding everything personally or relying on informal communication, begin to slow the company. New leaders join, culture shifts and conflict surfaces. Startups that develop leadership deliberately are better able to maintain speed and clarity through each stage of growth.

Investors want more than lagging revenue figures. Boards ask for evidence that the product is working, that growth is efficient and that the team can execute the next stage. Many startups report metrics that are easy to count rather than predictive. Current forces, including tighter capital, AI-native competitors and buyers who expect proof of value, raise the bar. Founders and investors who share behavior-based KPIs can have more honest conversations about progress, risk and where support will help most.

challenges.title: Traction signals buried in noise
challenges.body: Early datasets are small, inconsistent and shaped by founder involvement. Distinguishing genuine product pull from enthusiasm, discounts or one-time launches is hard. Teams may scale go-to-market spending before confirming which user behaviors predict retention, burning capital on growth that does not last.

challenges.title: Activation that is assumed, not validated
challenges.body: Startups often define activation by intuition or by convenient product events. Without validation against retention, onboarding is optimized for the wrong behaviors. Teams then struggle to explain why promising sign-ups fail to convert into active, paying customers who expand over time.

challenges.title: Founder bottlenecks as the team grows
challenges.body: Founders who made every decision in the early days can become bottlenecks as the company grows. Delegation feels risky, new leaders lack authority and communication that once happened naturally breaks down. The behaviors that built the company must evolve, and founders rarely have time or support to make that shift deliberately.

challenges.title: Investor reporting built on vanity metrics
challenges.body: Board decks often feature cumulative users, pipeline totals and top-line growth that look encouraging but say little about durability. When reported metrics do not predict outcomes, investors and founders lose time debating numbers instead of discussing decisions. Trust suffers when results eventually diverge from what dashboards implied.

challenges.title: Culture that forms by accident
challenges.body: Startup culture forms quickly through the behaviors leaders model and tolerate. Without attention, norms around feedback, accountability and inclusion develop by accident. Rapid hiring can dilute the qualities that made the early team effective, and cultural problems become harder to change once the company has scaled.

how_we_help.title: Activation and traction signals
how_we_help.body: We analyze product and customer data, even when it is sparse, to identify the early behaviors that predict retention and expansion. Behavioral Signals Design turns those findings into a validated activation definition, behavioral types and testable hypotheses, giving founders a clearer view of where the product is working and where it is not.

how_we_help.title: Founder and CEO coaching
how_we_help.body: We coach founders through the transitions that growth demands: delegating decisions, building a leadership team, managing the board and staying effective under pressure. Coaching draws on clinical psychology and executive coaching practice and is focused on specific behaviors the founder wants to change.

how_we_help.title: Predictive KPIs for boards and investors
how_we_help.body: We help founders and investors agree on a small set of behavior-based KPIs that predict revenue durability and efficient growth. Clear definitions and dashboards make board reporting more useful, focus conversations on decisions and give investors earlier insight into progress and risk across stages.

how_we_help.title: Venture capital advisory
how_we_help.body: For venture investors, we provide behavioral analysis of customer traction during evaluation and support for portfolio companies after investment. That includes assessing activation and retention signals, reviewing founder and team dynamics and helping portfolio companies establish measurement practices that make future rounds easier to evaluate.

how_we_help.title: Scaling leadership and culture
how_we_help.body: We work with startup leadership teams to define the behaviors that should carry through growth, design team routines that preserve speed and build psychological safety for honest debate. Team coaching helps new and founding leaders align on decisions and roles as the organization changes shape.

industries.impact_lens: Venture-backed startups bring new products, services and jobs into the world, and many address problems in health, education, climate and access to services. Behavioral science helps them do so responsibly: building products people genuinely value rather than products engineered for compulsive use, measuring progress honestly and developing leaders who create healthy workplaces as they scale. For investors, behavioral evidence supports better capital allocation toward companies that create real value. Founders who understand behavior are better equipped to build organizations and products that improve people's lives over the long term.

faqs.q: When should venture-backed startups invest in behavioral science?
faqs.a: Earlier than many expect. The most valuable time is when a startup is defining activation, preparing to scale go-to-market spending or building its first leadership team. At those points, small investments in identifying behavioral signals and developing leaders can prevent costly mistakes. Engagements are scoped to fit startup budgets and timelines.

faqs.q: Can you find meaningful signals in a small dataset?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Early datasets require careful methods: combining product data with qualitative research, focusing on cohorts and treating findings as hypotheses to test rather than settled conclusions. The goal is not statistical certainty at small scale but sharper, testable questions that help founders learn faster with each release and decide where to invest next.

faqs.q: Do you work with investors as well as founders?
faqs.a: Yes. We support venture investors in evaluating customer traction and team dynamics, and we work with portfolio companies after investment. When founders and investors share behavior-based KPIs, board conversations become more productive. We are clear about roles and confidentiality when working with both sides of the relationship, and we agree in writing what is shared with whom.

industries.name: Digital Health
industries.meta_title: Digital Health Engagement and Behavior Change Design
industries.meta_description: Improve digital health engagement with behavioral science: reduce engagement decay, support chronic illness self-management and build predictive KPIs.
industries.summary: Behavioral design and analytics for digital health companies working to sustain engagement, support chronic illness self-management and prove clinical and commercial value.
industries.lede: Digital health engagement tends to peak early and fade quietly. We help digital health companies understand why users drift, design products that support lasting self-management and define predictive KPIs that connect daily behavior to clinical and commercial outcomes.
context: Digital health products promise continuous support for conditions that unfold over years: diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, chronic pain, depression and anxiety. The pattern most teams know well is engagement decay. Users enroll with real motivation, log readings and complete lessons for a few weeks, then open the app less often until they stop. The product has not failed technically. It has asked people to sustain a new behavior without enough attention to ability, timing and meaning in the context of their lives.

Inside the company, product, clinical, data science and commercial teams often hold different definitions of success. Clinicians care about outcomes and safety, product teams track active users and feature use, and sales teams need evidence that employers, health plans and providers will accept. Without shared, behavior-based KPIs, teams optimize for different signals, and the engagement metrics that look healthy on dashboards may have little relationship to whether members actually manage their condition better.

The market has matured. Buyers now expect evidence of sustained use and measurable health improvement, not download counts. Integration with care teams, remote monitoring devices and payer workflows adds complexity. AI coaching and personalization create new possibilities and new ethical questions about persuasion. Companies that understand digital health engagement as a behavioral science problem, and measure it accordingly, are better positioned to retain members, earn clinical trust and demonstrate value to the organizations that pay for them.

challenges.title: Engagement decay after the first weeks
challenges.body: Early enthusiasm carries new users through onboarding, then real life intervenes. Notifications become noise, logging feels like a chore and progress stalls. Teams often respond with more content or more reminders, which can accelerate disengagement. The underlying question, which behaviors predict who will persist, usually goes unanswered because the data has not been examined through a behavioral lens.

challenges.title: Self-management that does not fit daily life
challenges.body: Chronic illness self-management asks people to monitor, adjust medication, change diet and stay active, often while managing work, family and fatigue. Products designed around an ideal user overlook the routines and constraints of real patients. When the recommended behavior is too hard or poorly timed, even motivated members fall away and blame themselves.

challenges.title: Vanity metrics that buyers do not trust
challenges.body: Daily active users, session counts and content completion are easy to report and hard to connect with health outcomes. Employers, health plans and provider partners increasingly ask for evidence that engagement translates into better control of a condition. Without predictive KPIs that link behavior to outcomes, renewal conversations rely on narrative rather than proof.

challenges.title: Onboarding that loses people before value appears
challenges.body: Many digital health products ask for device pairing, health history, goals and permissions before members experience any benefit. Each step is a chance to drop off. Onboarding often reflects internal requirements instead of the user's first meaningful win, which means the people who most need support may never reach it.

challenges.title: Persuasion without clear ethical boundaries
challenges.body: Streaks, rewards, social features and AI coaches can motivate healthy behavior, but they can also create pressure, guilt or dependence. Digital health teams need principles for when persuasion supports a person's own goals and when it crosses into manipulation, especially for vulnerable populations living with serious or stigmatized conditions.

how_we_help.title: Engagement signals and behavioral types
how_we_help.body: We analyze product event data alongside clinical and enrollment data to find the early behaviors that predict persistence and the points where members drift. Behavioral segmentation then groups users by how they engage, not by demographics, so teams can design different pathways for the people who need structure, those who need flexibility and those who need human contact.

how_we_help.title: Self-management product design
how_we_help.body: Drawing on clinical health psychology and behavioral medicine, we redesign core routines such as logging, medication tracking and activity goals so they fit real lives. That means smaller starting behaviors, better anchoring to existing habits and prompts that arrive when a person can act. Each change is framed as a testable hypothesis rather than a feature request.

how_we_help.title: Onboarding and first-value design
how_we_help.body: We map onboarding step by step, measure where members leave and redesign the sequence around a first meaningful win, such as a useful insight from a first reading. Usability testing with representative patients surfaces confusion early, and A/B tests confirm which changes improve activation without sacrificing data quality or clinical safety.

how_we_help.title: Outcome-linked predictive KPIs
how_we_help.body: We help product, clinical and commercial teams agree on a small set of behavior-based KPIs that predict health outcomes and renewal. These measures give leaders an earlier, more credible view of program performance and give buyers evidence they can evaluate. Dashboards make the measures usable in weekly decisions rather than quarterly reports.

how_we_help.title: Ethical persuasive technology review
how_we_help.body: We review engagement mechanics, messaging and AI coaching behavior against principles from persuasive technology and self-determination theory. The review identifies features that support autonomy and competence and flags those that may create pressure or shame. Teams leave with practical design standards they can apply to future features and experiments.

industries.impact_lens: Digital health can extend support to people who live far from specialists, cannot take time off for frequent visits or feel stigma about seeking care. That promise is realized only if people keep using the product long enough for it to help. Behavioral science advances the mission by designing for real lives, sustaining engagement through meaning and competence rather than pressure, and measuring whether daily behavior actually improves health. It also keeps persuasion honest, ensuring that technology helps people pursue their own goals for managing chronic illness with dignity.

faqs.q: Why does digital health engagement drop off, and can it be prevented?
faqs.a: Drop-off usually reflects a mismatch between what the product asks and what people can sustain in their daily lives. Some decline is natural as members build routines, so the goal is not constant use but the right behaviors at the right frequency. We identify which early behaviors predict persistence and design pathways that support them. No approach eliminates attrition, but it can be understood, measured and reduced through testing.

faqs.q: Do you work with clinical teams as well as product teams?
faqs.a: Yes. Our roots are in clinical and health psychology and behavioral medicine, so we are comfortable working with medical directors, clinical researchers and care coaches alongside product managers, designers and data scientists. Much of the value comes from aligning these groups on shared, behavior-based measures of success that respect clinical evidence and product realities.

faqs.q: Can behavioral science help us show value to employers and health plans?
faqs.a: It can help you build a more credible case. We define predictive KPIs that link member behavior to health outcomes and design experiments that isolate the effect of specific product features. That evidence supports renewal and sales conversations with buyers who want more than engagement counts. We do not promise particular outcomes, but we help you measure them rigorously.

industries.name: Fitness, Health Clubs & Wellness
industries.meta_title: Fitness Member Retention and Behavioral Science
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science for fitness member retention: reduce churn, close the gap between benefits and perception, and build engagement KPIs for health clubs.
industries.summary: Behavioral science for health clubs, studios and wellness brands focused on fitness member retention, early habit formation and closing the gap between real benefits and perception.
industries.lede: Fitness member retention is decided early, often in the first weeks after joining. We help health clubs, studios and wellness brands find the behaviors that predict who stays, design experiences that build lasting habits and communicate value people believe.
context: The fitness industry sells something people genuinely want: better health, more energy, a stronger body and a sense of belonging. Yet member churn remains a persistent challenge. Many new members join with high motivation and visit often for a short period, then their attendance tapers as schedules, discomfort or self-consciousness intervene. Cancellation is the final event in a story that began weeks earlier with fewer visits, and most clubs see the ending in their data long after they could have changed it.

There is also a gap between the benefits the industry delivers and how consumers perceive it. Regular exercise supports cardiovascular health, mood, sleep and healthy aging, but many people associate gyms with intimidation, judgment or a body ideal that feels out of reach. Messaging that emphasizes transformation can widen that gap for the people who would benefit most. Inside clubs, front-desk staff, trainers and managers are central to member experience, yet they are often measured on sales rather than on the early behaviors that drive retention.

Current forces are reshaping the sector: hybrid digital and in-person offerings, wearable data, boutique and low-cost models competing for the same members, and growing interest in healthy aging and mental wellbeing. Clubs and wellness brands that understand fitness member retention as a behavioral problem, and that design for habit formation, belonging and perceived competence, are better positioned to keep members and to broaden who sees fitness as something for them.

challenges.title: Churn that starts long before cancellation
challenges.body: Most clubs treat cancellation as the event to prevent, but disengagement begins with small changes: a skipped week, a shorter visit or a class no longer attended. Without early behavioral signals, retention efforts arrive too late. Save offers at the point of cancellation address the symptom and miss the habit that never formed.

challenges.title: The perception gap around fitness
challenges.body: The industry delivers real health and wellbeing benefits, yet many consumers perceive gyms as intimidating, expensive or meant for people already fit. Marketing that relies on dramatic transformations can reinforce that perception. Closing the gap requires messaging tested with the audiences the industry has not yet reached, not only with existing enthusiasts.

challenges.title: Onboarding that ends at the sale
challenges.body: New members often receive a tour, a contract and perhaps a single trainer session. After that, they are left to build a routine alone in an unfamiliar environment. The first weeks are when competence, comfort and social connection are formed or lost, and many clubs have no designed experience for that period.

challenges.title: Staff incentives misaligned with retention
challenges.body: Front-desk teams, trainers and managers shape whether members feel welcomed and capable. When incentives reward new sales and personal training packages, early member experience becomes nobody's job. Leaders need measures and coaching that connect frontline behavior with the member behaviors that predict long-term retention.

challenges.title: Digital and wearable data left unused
challenges.body: Check-in systems, apps, class bookings and wearables generate rich behavioral data, but it often sits in separate platforms. Clubs report attendance totals without understanding visit patterns, class sequences or social ties that distinguish members who stay. The signals exist. They have not been integrated or interpreted through behavioral science.

how_we_help.title: Early churn signal analysis
how_we_help.body: We combine check-in, booking, app, billing and survey data to identify the visit patterns and behavioral types that predict retention or lapse. The result is a short list of early warning signals and predictive KPIs that club leaders can monitor weekly, along with hypotheses about which interventions might change the trajectory for each type of member.

how_we_help.title: First-90-days experience design
how_we_help.body: We design the new member journey around habit formation, perceived competence and belonging. That may include a structured first month, smaller starting goals, buddy or class pathways and well-timed staff check-ins. Each element is tied to a behavioral moment that the data suggests matters, and each is piloted before broad rollout.

how_we_help.title: Industry and brand perception research
how_we_help.body: We research how prospective members, lapsed members and non-exercisers perceive fitness and specific brands. Messaging concepts are then tested for credibility, inclusiveness and motivation, with attention to audiences who feel the industry is not for them. The aim is communication that conveys real benefits without relying on intimidation or unrealistic ideals.

how_we_help.title: Retention strategy and frontline coaching
how_we_help.body: We help leaders build a retention strategy around predictive member behaviors and align staff roles, scripts and incentives with it. Coaching for managers and frontline teams focuses on the specific interactions that help members feel known and capable, and dashboards show each location how its early member behaviors are trending.

how_we_help.title: Fitness and wellness industry advisory
how_we_help.body: For operators, suppliers, investors and industry bodies, we provide advisory grounded in behavioral science and health psychology. Topics include hybrid offering strategy, wearable and app integration, healthy aging programs and how to frame the public health value of exercise in ways consumers find credible and motivating.

industries.impact_lens: Regular physical activity is one of the most powerful tools for preventing chronic disease and supporting mental health, and fitness and wellness businesses are a primary place where people try to build that habit. When members drop out, they lose more than a membership. Behavioral science advances the sector's social good by helping more people form lasting routines, feel welcome in spaces that once seemed intimidating and understand the real benefits of activity. It also encourages honest communication that broadens participation rather than reinforcing narrow ideals of who belongs in fitness.

faqs.q: What drives fitness member retention most?
faqs.a: The specific drivers vary by club model and member population, which is why we analyze each operator's own data. In general, retention depends on whether members form a routine early, feel competent in the environment and experience some social connection. We identify the behaviors that predict retention for your members, such as visit regularity or class participation, and design interventions to strengthen them.

faqs.q: Can you help us reach people who do not currently exercise?
faqs.a: Yes. Many people perceive gyms as intimidating or not designed for them. We research those perceptions with prospective and lapsed members and non-exercisers, then test messaging and entry experiences that lower barriers. The aim is to communicate the real benefits of activity in ways that feel credible and welcoming rather than relying on transformation imagery.

faqs.q: Do we need a sophisticated data platform to start?
faqs.a: No. Most clubs already have check-in, billing and booking data that contain useful behavioral signals. We start with what exists, integrate it pragmatically and identify the few measures worth tracking. If additional data, such as wearable or app events, would add predictive value, we recommend it based on evidence rather than assuming more data is always better.

industries.name: Automotive
industries.meta_title: Automotive Owner Experience and Behavioral Science
industries.meta_description: Improve the automotive owner experience with behavioral science: connected-car feature adoption, dealer handoffs and customer experience center performance.
industries.summary: Behavioral science for automakers improving the owner experience across connected-car technology, customer experience centers, dealer handoffs and adoption of in-vehicle features.
industries.lede: The automotive owner experience now extends far beyond the showroom, into apps, connected services, contact centers and the dealer service lane. We help automakers read the behavioral signals across that journey and design for adoption, loyalty and trust.
context: Buying a vehicle used to be the defining moment of the relationship between a brand and its customer. Today, the automotive owner experience continues for years through connected-car apps, over-the-air updates, subscription features, customer experience centers and dealer service visits. Each touchpoint generates data, and each one can either strengthen or weaken the owner's sense that the brand understands them. Most automakers hold that data in separate systems owned by separate teams, which makes the full owner journey difficult to see.

Technology feature adoption is a particular challenge. Vehicles ship with driver assistance, connected navigation, remote start, charging management and safety features that many owners never activate or fully understand. The reasons are behavioral: features are introduced at delivery when the owner is overwhelmed, menus are complex and the value is not obvious until a relevant moment arrives. Inside the organization, product, digital, customer experience and dealer network teams each hold part of the problem and are measured on different outcomes.

Handoffs are where experience most often breaks. The dealer sells the vehicle, the brand owns the app, the contact center answers questions and the service lane handles maintenance. Owners do not see those boundaries and expect continuity. Electrification adds new questions about charging, range and ownership costs, while connected services shift revenue toward ongoing relationships. Automakers that treat the owner experience as a designed, measured behavioral journey are better positioned to earn loyalty at the next purchase.

challenges.title: Connected features that owners never activate
challenges.body: Many owners leave the dealership without pairing the app, enabling connected services or learning the driver assistance features they paid for. Delivery is crowded with paperwork and emotion, which is a poor moment for learning. Low activation reduces perceived value, limits data and weakens the case for subscription services and future connected offerings.

challenges.title: Dealer handoffs that break continuity
challenges.body: Owners experience the brand and the dealer as one relationship, but data, incentives and accountability are split between them. Information captured at sale may not reach the app or contact center, and service visits may ignore digital history. These gaps create repeated questions, inconsistent answers and frustration that owners attribute to the brand.

challenges.title: Customer experience centers measured on speed
challenges.body: Contact and customer experience centers are often managed to handle time and satisfaction scores. Those measures say little about whether an owner's problem was actually resolved or whether the conversation increased loyalty and feature use. Agents lack the behavioral insight and authority to turn a support call into a better ownership experience.

challenges.title: Owner data spread across many systems
challenges.body: Telematics, app events, dealer management systems, warranty records, contact center logs and surveys each describe part of the owner journey. Integrating them is technically and organizationally hard, so decisions rely on assumptions about what owners value. The behavioral moments that predict repurchase and advocacy remain hidden in the noise.

challenges.title: Electrification and new ownership questions
challenges.body: Electric vehicle owners face unfamiliar decisions about home charging, public networks, range planning and battery care. Early experiences shape confidence and word of mouth. When guidance is generic or arrives too late, owners fill gaps with anxiety and anecdote, and the brand misses a chance to build trust during a pivotal transition.

how_we_help.title: Owner journey mapping across touchpoints
how_we_help.body: We map the full automotive owner experience from purchase through delivery, early ownership, service and repurchase, including the handoffs between brand, dealer, app and contact center. Interviews and contextual research with owners and frontline staff reveal where continuity breaks, and data analysis shows which moments carry the most weight for loyalty.

how_we_help.title: Technology feature adoption strategy
how_we_help.body: We identify which connected and in-vehicle features matter most to owners and why adoption stalls. Interventions are designed around timing and ability: introducing features at relevant moments, simplifying first use and prompting through the app or vehicle when value is clear. Each approach is tested with owner cohorts before scaling across models or markets.

how_we_help.title: Experience center performance and coaching
how_we_help.body: For an automaker's owner-experience or customer experience center, we define behavior-based KPIs that capture resolution, feature adoption and loyalty signals rather than speed alone. We then design conversation guides and coach supervisors and teams so agents can turn routine contacts into moments that strengthen the ownership relationship.

how_we_help.title: Dealer handoff service design
how_we_help.body: We design the handoff points between dealer and brand, such as delivery, first service and app onboarding, so information and responsibility move with the owner. Service blueprints clarify roles, data flows and the specific behaviors expected from each party, and pilots with participating dealers test whether the redesigned handoffs improve owner outcomes.

how_we_help.title: In-vehicle and app usability research
how_we_help.body: Drawing on human-computer interaction principles, we test in-vehicle interfaces, companion apps and onboarding flows with representative owners. Research surfaces the confusion that suppresses feature use and the design changes most likely to improve it. Findings are prioritized by their likely effect on adoption, safety and satisfaction.

industries.impact_lens: Vehicles are woven into how people reach work, care for family and stay connected to community, and many of the most important safety and efficiency gains now depend on whether owners understand and use available technology. Behavioral science advances the public good in automotive by helping owners adopt safety features with confidence, navigate the transition to electrified vehicles and receive consistent, respectful support. Designing technology around real human attention and ability reduces frustration and risk, and it builds trust that owners carry into every interaction with the brand and its dealers.

faqs.q: Why do owners not use connected-car features they paid for?
faqs.a: Usually because the features were introduced at the wrong moment or demand more effort than owners expect. Delivery is busy and emotional, menus can be complex and the value of many features becomes clear only in a specific situation. We study where adoption stalls and design prompts, simplified first use and timely education that help owners discover features when they are most relevant.

faqs.q: Can you work across both the brand and the dealer network?
faqs.a: Yes. Much of the automotive owner experience depends on handoffs between the brand, dealers, contact centers and digital channels. We map those relationships, involve dealer staff in research and design, and pilot changes with participating dealers. The goal is a consistent experience that respects each party's role while making accountability for the owner clear.

faqs.q: What does a customer experience center engagement involve?
faqs.a: We observe interactions, analyze contact and owner data, and identify which conversation behaviors predict resolution, feature adoption and loyalty. We then define predictive KPIs, design guides and coaching for supervisors and agents, and test changes with selected teams. The work aims to make the center a source of insight about owners, not only a place where issues are closed.

industries.name: Mortgage & Consumer Lending
industries.meta_title: Mortgage Borrower Experience and Behavioral Science
industries.meta_description: Improve the mortgage borrower experience with behavioral science: close data gaps between application and closing, raise engagement and retain borrowers.
industries.summary: Behavioral science for lenders improving the mortgage borrower experience, from first inquiry through application, closing and the long relationship that follows.
industries.lede: The mortgage borrower experience is long, emotional and full of data gaps. We help mortgage and consumer lenders understand borrower behavior between application and closing, and after it, so they can design for confidence, completion and lasting relationships.
context: For most homebuyers, a mortgage is the largest financial commitment they will make, and it arrives during an already stressful life event. The journey from first inquiry to closing involves rate shopping, documentation, appraisal, underwriting conditions and coordination with agents, title companies and sellers. Borrowers experience uncertainty at every step. When they do not understand what is happening or what they need to do next, they delay, disengage or switch lenders, and loan officers spend their time chasing documents instead of advising.

Lenders face a distinctive data problem. Between application and closing there are long stretches where borrower behavior is barely visible, and after closing the relationship often goes quiet until a refinance or next purchase, when the borrower may not return. Point-of-sale systems, loan origination platforms, customer relationship tools, servicing and marketing each capture fragments. Without an integrated behavioral view, lenders rely on assumptions about why borrowers fall out, what drives recapture and which communications actually help.

Rate cycles, affordability pressures and digital-first competitors make these questions urgent. Volume swings test whether teams can maintain experience quality, and first-time buyers often need more guidance than processes assume. Inside lending organizations, loan officers, processors, underwriters and marketing teams are measured on different outcomes. Lenders that treat the mortgage borrower experience as a behavioral journey, with predictive measures for each stage, can improve pull-through, borrower confidence and long-term retention without relying on rate alone.

challenges.title: Silent gaps between application and closing
challenges.body: After a borrower applies, weeks can pass with only sporadic contact while underwriting proceeds. Borrowers in that gap wonder whether things are on track, respond slowly to condition requests and may entertain competing offers. Lenders often lack signals that a borrower is losing confidence until the loan is delayed or withdrawn.

challenges.title: Document requests that stall progress
challenges.body: Requests for pay stubs, statements and explanations are a major source of friction. Borrowers may not understand why something is needed, where to find it or how to submit it. Each round of back and forth extends timelines and frustrates everyone involved, yet the requests are rarely designed with behavioral principles in mind.

challenges.title: Relationships that go quiet after closing
challenges.body: Once the loan closes, many lenders have little meaningful contact with borrowers until a refinance or new purchase is possible. By then the borrower may not remember the lender or may associate it with stress. Long post-close data gaps make it difficult to know who is likely to return and what would earn that return.

challenges.title: First-time buyers who need more guidance
challenges.body: First-time homebuyers often feel uncertain about credit, down payments and the process itself. Standard communications assume familiarity they may not have. Without designed support, these borrowers are more likely to delay, make costly mistakes or give up, which is a loss for both the household and the lender.

challenges.title: Loan teams measured on different outcomes
challenges.body: Loan officers, processors, underwriters, closers and marketers each own part of the borrower experience but are judged by different metrics. Handoffs create delays and inconsistent messages. Leaders struggle to align teams around the borrower behaviors that predict funded loans, satisfaction and referral, rather than around separate departmental targets.

how_we_help.title: Homebuyer journey mapping
how_we_help.body: We map the homebuyer journey from first inquiry through application, processing, closing and the years after, including interactions with agents and third parties. Borrower and loan team interviews reveal moments of confusion and anxiety, while data analysis shows where borrowers stall or fall out. The map becomes a shared reference for teams that usually see only their own stage.

how_we_help.title: Signals for the data gaps
how_we_help.body: Using Behavioral Signals Design, we connect point-of-sale, origination, CRM and servicing data to find behaviors that predict pull-through, delay and future return. Where data is missing, we make the underlying assumptions explicit and define testable hypotheses. The outcome is a short set of predictive KPIs for each stage of the borrower relationship.

how_we_help.title: Borrower communication and engagement design
how_we_help.body: We redesign status updates, condition requests and educational content around what borrowers need to act. Clear next steps, better timing and reassurance during quiet periods can reduce uncertainty and speed responses. Messages are tested through controlled comparisons so lenders know which changes actually improve engagement and completion.

how_we_help.title: Post-close retention strategy
how_we_help.body: We help lenders design a post-close relationship that is useful rather than promotional, with communication tied to life events, homeownership milestones and financial health. Behavioral segmentation identifies which borrowers are most likely to need help next, and experiments test which forms of contact build enough trust for a borrower to return.

how_we_help.title: Loan process mapping and team alignment
how_we_help.body: We map the operational process behind the borrower experience, identify handoffs that create delay and redesign roles around shared borrower outcomes. Leadership alignment sessions and team coaching help loan officers, processors and underwriters work from common measures, so improvement efforts reinforce one another instead of competing.

industries.impact_lens: Homeownership is a primary path to household stability and wealth for many families, and the mortgage process can either open that path or make it feel unreachable. Behavioral science advances the social good in lending by making complex financial decisions more understandable, reducing the anxiety that leads qualified borrowers to give up and supporting first-time buyers who lack experienced guidance. It also encourages responsible persuasion: communication that helps borrowers make informed choices aligned with their own interests, rather than pressure that serves short-term volume at the borrower's expense.

faqs.q: How can behavioral science improve the mortgage borrower experience?
faqs.a: It focuses attention on the specific behaviors that move a loan forward, such as responding to condition requests, locking a rate or scheduling an appraisal, and on the uncertainty that slows them. By mapping the journey, finding predictive signals in existing data and testing better communications, lenders can reduce friction and anxiety. Results depend on each lender's context, so changes are tested before scaling.

faqs.q: What do you mean by data gaps in the mortgage journey?
faqs.a: There are long periods, particularly during underwriting and after closing, when lenders have little visibility into borrower behavior or sentiment. Decisions about outreach and recapture are then based on assumptions. We identify where those gaps occur, what signals can fill them and which assumptions need to be tested, so teams can act earlier and with more confidence.

faqs.q: Do you work with consumer lenders outside mortgage?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of the same principles apply to personal loans, auto finance and home equity products: complex decisions, documentation friction and relationships that fade after funding. We adapt the approach to each product's journey and regulatory context, always with an emphasis on informed borrower choice and on measures that reflect the borrower's long-term financial wellbeing.

industries.name: Banking & Financial Services
industries.meta_title: Behavioral Science in Banking and Financial Services
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science in banking: improve digital adoption, customer financial wellbeing, relationship deepening and frontline performance with tested design.
industries.summary: Behavioral science in banking and financial services for institutions improving digital adoption, customer financial wellbeing, relationship deepening and frontline team performance.
industries.lede: Behavioral science in banking recognizes that money decisions are rarely purely rational. We help banks, credit unions and financial services firms understand customer behavior, design for better financial choices and build teams that deepen relationships responsibly.
context: Financial decisions are shaped by emotion, habit, attention and trust as much as by interest rates and fees. Customers delay opening savings accounts, avoid looking at balances when worried, accept default options and stay with institutions out of inertia. These patterns matter both to customer wellbeing and to institutional performance. Behavioral science in banking offers a way to understand them and to design products and experiences that help people act on intentions they already hold, such as saving more or borrowing wisely.

Inside banks and credit unions, the people problems are equally significant. Branch staff, relationship managers and contact center teams are asked to shift from transactions to advice, often with incentives and tools built for an earlier era. Digital and branch channels compete instead of complementing each other. Customer data is plentiful, yet it sits in core banking, card, digital banking, CRM and marketing platforms that rarely produce an integrated view of behavior. Leaders make decisions about relationship deepening on assumptions rather than tested evidence.

Current forces intensify the challenge: digital-first competitors, rising expectations for personalized service, growing attention to financial health and fair treatment, and AI tools that can personalize outreach at scale. Each of these creates opportunities and risks. Institutions that apply behavioral science carefully can raise digital adoption, deepen relationships and support financial wellbeing while maintaining the trust that distinguishes a responsible financial partner. Those that apply it carelessly risk eroding that trust quickly.

challenges.title: Digital adoption that plateaus
challenges.body: Many customers open a mobile app once, then return to branches or call centers for tasks they could complete digitally. Adoption stalls when features feel unfamiliar, security steps are confusing or customers lack confidence. Campaigns that simply promote the app rarely change habits formed over years of in-person banking.

challenges.title: Relationship deepening that feels like selling
challenges.body: Institutions want customers to hold more products, but customers resist when offers feel irrelevant or pushy. Cross-sell programs built on product targets can erode trust. The behavioral question is how to recognize genuine needs and present options at moments when customers are ready to consider them.

challenges.title: Customer financial wellbeing as a measure
challenges.body: Many institutions want to support customer financial health, but measuring it is difficult and connecting it to business outcomes is harder still. Without credible measures, financial wellbeing initiatives remain marketing themes rather than design principles that shape products, communications and frontline conversations.

challenges.title: Frontline roles in transition
challenges.body: Branch and contact center staff are being asked to advise rather than process, often without clear guidance, coaching or aligned incentives. Many feel uncertain about how to start needs-based conversations. Leaders need a clear picture of the behaviors that define effective advice and a way to develop them consistently.

challenges.title: Fragmented customer data
challenges.body: Core banking, card, lending, digital and CRM systems each describe part of a customer's financial life. Without integration around behavioral signals, institutions miss early indicators of attrition, financial stress or readiness for new products. Analysts default to demographic segments that explain little about how customers actually behave.

how_we_help.title: Behavioral segmentation for banking
how_we_help.body: We analyze transaction, channel and product data to define behavioral types, such as digital-ready customers who still visit branches or savers who avoid planning tools. These segments explain behavior better than demographics and guide where to focus design and outreach. Each segment comes with testable hypotheses about what would help those customers.

how_we_help.title: Digital banking adoption design
how_we_help.body: We study why customers do not adopt digital tools and design interventions around confidence, ability and timing. Examples include assisted first use in branches, simplified security steps and prompts linked to tasks customers already perform. Pilots measure sustained digital behavior rather than downloads, so leaders know which approaches change habits.

how_we_help.title: Needs-based relationship deepening
how_we_help.body: We help institutions redesign cross-sell around customer needs and life moments, aligning frontline conversations, digital prompts and incentives. The approach draws on the psychology of trust and decision-making and is tested against both product outcomes and customer satisfaction, so deeper relationships are earned rather than pushed.

how_we_help.title: Financial wellbeing measurement
how_we_help.body: Applying psychometrics and survey design, we help institutions build credible measures of customer financial wellbeing and link them with behavioral data. These measures support product decisions, communications and frontline coaching, and they give leaders a way to track whether initiatives actually improve customers' financial lives.

how_we_help.title: Frontline leadership and team coaching
how_we_help.body: We coach branch and contact center leaders to develop advice-oriented teams, using observation and data to identify the conversation behaviors that matter. Team coaching builds psychological safety and practice routines so staff can try new approaches, learn from them and improve together over time.

industries.impact_lens: Financial institutions influence whether households can save, borrow responsibly, weather emergencies and plan for the future. Behavioral science advances that social good by designing products and conversations that help people follow through on their own financial intentions, such as building savings or avoiding costly fees. It also brings rigor to measuring financial wellbeing and guards against persuasion that benefits the institution at the customer's expense. Applied responsibly, behavioral science in banking aligns long-term institutional performance with the financial resilience of the customers and communities the institution serves.

faqs.q: How is behavioral science in banking different from traditional marketing analytics?
faqs.a: Marketing analytics often focuses on who to target and which offer to send. Behavioral science in banking begins with the customer behavior that matters, such as saving regularly or adopting digital tools, and asks what motivation, ability and prompts shape it. Interventions may involve product design, frontline conversations or defaults as well as messaging, and they are tested experimentally.

faqs.q: Do you work with credit unions and community banks?
faqs.a: Yes. Credit unions and community banks often have strong relationships and member-focused missions, along with data spread across core and digital systems. We adapt our methods to their scale, starting with existing data and practical pilots. Their emphasis on member wellbeing aligns naturally with an ethical approach to behavioral design.

faqs.q: How do you ensure behavioral design is used ethically in financial services?
faqs.a: We design to help customers act on their own goals, not to exploit biases for short-term gain. That means transparent choices, defaults that serve customer interests and measures that include customer outcomes alongside institutional ones. We review interventions for potential harm, particularly for financially vulnerable customers, before they are tested or scaled.

industries.name: Commercial Real Estate & Capital Markets
industries.meta_title: Commercial Real Estate Cross-Selling and Growth
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science for commercial real estate cross-selling: connect service lines, strengthen relationship-driven sales and build predictive pipeline KPIs.
industries.summary: Behavioral science for commercial real estate and capital markets firms improving cross-selling between service lines, relationship-driven sales and the leadership behaviors behind growth.
industries.lede: Commercial real estate cross-selling depends less on org charts than on trust between producers. We help capital markets and real estate services firms understand the behaviors behind referrals and relationship-driven sales, then design processes that make collaboration natural.
context: Commercial real estate and capital markets firms often offer a broad platform: debt and equity placement, investment sales, leasing, valuation, property management and advisory. Clients could benefit from more of that platform, and firms invest in integration to make it happen. Yet commercial real estate cross-selling frequently disappoints. Producers protect relationships they have built over years, worry about service quality in unfamiliar lines and lack a clear picture of what colleagues in other groups actually do. The barriers are behavioral before they are structural.

Sales in this sector are relationship-driven. Deals depend on trust, timing and market knowledge held by individual brokers and bankers. Referral behavior is shaped by reputation, reciprocity and perceived risk. Leaders often rely on incentive splits and mandates to drive collaboration, then find that the behavior they want does not follow. Meanwhile, CRM data is incomplete because producers see little reason to enter it, which leaves leadership making growth decisions with partial information.

Current forces add pressure. Capital markets cycles shift activity across service lines, making cross-referral a source of resilience. Clients increasingly expect integrated advice across their portfolios. Consolidation brings teams with different cultures under one brand. Technology and AI tools promise better pipeline visibility but depend on adoption by busy producers. Firms that understand the psychology of relationship-driven sales and measure the right leading behaviors can build collaboration that holds through market cycles.

challenges.title: Producers who protect their relationships
challenges.body: A broker or banker's client relationships represent years of work and personal reputation. Introducing a colleague from another service line feels risky if the producer cannot vouch for the outcome. Without trust between groups, cross-selling programs produce meetings and presentations but few genuine referrals that clients welcome.

challenges.title: Incentives that do not change behavior
challenges.body: Firms often adjust fee splits or set referral targets to encourage collaboration. Incentives matter, but they rarely overcome concerns about client experience, unclear processes or unfamiliarity with colleagues. When the incentive becomes the main lever, producers may refer superficially or game the system rather than collaborate in ways clients value.

challenges.title: Limited visibility into the pipeline
challenges.body: CRM systems in commercial real estate are often incomplete because producers see entry as administrative overhead. Leaders lack reliable signals about which relationships span service lines, where referrals originate and which interactions precede closed business. Growth strategy relies on lagging revenue figures and anecdote rather than predictive measures.

challenges.title: Integrating cultures after combinations
challenges.body: Mergers and team acquisitions bring groups with different norms around sharing information, splitting fees and serving clients. Leaders may announce an integrated platform while day-to-day behavior stays siloed. Without attention to culture and trust, the expected collaboration benefits of a combination are slow to appear.

challenges.title: Clients who see fragments of the platform
challenges.body: Clients often know a firm through one producer and one service line. They may not realize the firm could help with financing, leasing or valuation elsewhere in their portfolio. When integrated advice is not offered at the right moment, clients engage competitors and the firm's broader capabilities remain underused.

how_we_help.title: Cross-sell process design
how_we_help.body: We study how referrals actually happen in your firm, through interviews with producers and analysis of deal and CRM data, and identify the moments where collaboration succeeds or stalls. We then design a cross-sell process around trust, clear handoffs and client value, with roles and routines that producers find practical rather than bureaucratic.

how_we_help.title: Predictive pipeline KPIs
how_we_help.body: Using Behavioral Signals Design, we identify the producer and client behaviors that precede cross-line business, such as joint client meetings or shared market updates. These become predictive KPIs that leaders can track before revenue appears, giving earlier insight into whether collaboration initiatives are working and where to intervene.

how_we_help.title: Leadership alignment for integrated growth
how_we_help.body: Service line leaders often agree on integration in principle and differ in practice. We facilitate alignment on shared goals, decision rights and the specific behaviors expected from leaders, then coach them to model collaboration. Alignment work is grounded in data about current referral patterns so conversations stay concrete.

how_we_help.title: Client experience research
how_we_help.body: We interview clients about how they experience the firm across service lines, what they value in advice and when they would welcome introductions to colleagues. Findings inform both cross-sell design and messaging, ensuring that collaboration is framed around client needs rather than internal revenue goals.

how_we_help.title: CRM and technology adoption
how_we_help.body: We treat CRM and pipeline tool adoption as a behavioral design challenge. By reducing entry effort, showing producers personal value from the data and aligning tools with existing routines, firms can improve data quality without relying on mandates. Changes are piloted with selected teams and measured before broader rollout.

industries.impact_lens: Commercial real estate and capital markets shape where people work, shop, receive care and live, and the financing behind those properties influences the vitality of communities. Behavioral science contributes by improving how firms collaborate to give clients sound, integrated advice, which supports better investment and property decisions. It also strengthens the professional cultures behind that advice, rewarding trust and knowledge sharing over territorial behavior. When firms understand the human side of relationship-driven sales, they serve clients more completely and build organizations that remain resilient through market cycles.

faqs.q: Why does commercial real estate cross-selling often underperform?
faqs.a: Because it depends on producers trusting colleagues with relationships they value highly. Incentives and mandates do not resolve concerns about client experience, unclear handoffs or unfamiliarity with other service lines. We address these behavioral barriers directly, designing processes and leadership practices that make referral feel safe and beneficial for producers and clients alike.

faqs.q: How do you measure collaboration before it shows up in revenue?
faqs.a: We identify leading behaviors that precede cross-line business, such as joint pitches, shared client meetings and documented introductions, and validate them against historical deal data where possible. These predictive KPIs let leaders see whether collaboration is growing months before fees are recognized, and they highlight which teams or offices need support.

faqs.q: Do you work with capital markets teams specifically?
faqs.a: Yes. Debt and equity advisory teams have distinctive relationship dynamics and are often central to cross-line opportunities, since financing touches many other services. We work with capital markets leaders and producers to understand referral patterns, client expectations and the coordination required to deliver integrated advice across a firm's platform, from first introduction through closing.

industries.name: Higher Education & Research
industries.meta_title: Student Engagement in Higher Education, by Design
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science for student engagement in higher education: improve persistence, belonging, faculty effectiveness and research translation with evidence.
industries.summary: Behavioral science for colleges, universities and research institutions improving student engagement in higher education, belonging, faculty effectiveness and the translation of research into practice.
industries.lede: Student engagement in higher education shapes persistence, learning and wellbeing, yet it is often measured too late to act on. We help institutions read early behavioral signals, design for belonging and support faculty and leaders through change.
context: Colleges and universities hold rich data about students: admissions records, learning management system activity, advising notes, financial aid, housing and survey results. Yet student engagement in higher education is often understood only through end-of-term grades and retention reports. By the time a student withdraws, the behavioral signals that preceded the decision, such as fewer logins, missed advising appointments or withdrawal from campus activities, have usually been visible for weeks in systems no one integrated.

Belonging is central. Students who feel they matter to faculty and peers are more likely to seek help, persist through setbacks and engage deeply with learning. First-generation students, transfer students, adult learners and students from underrepresented groups may face additional barriers to that sense of belonging. Inside the institution, faculty carry teaching, research and service loads, advisors manage large caseloads and leaders navigate shared governance. Change initiatives often stall because they ask busy people to adopt new practices without designing for their reality.

Current forces add urgency: demographic shifts in the college-age population, public questions about value, growing mental health needs, hybrid and online learning, and AI tools that change how students study and how faculty teach. Research institutions face an additional challenge in translating discoveries into accessible knowledge and practice. Institutions that approach these issues with behavioral science, grounded in learning research and measurement, can make better decisions and support both learners and the people who teach them.

challenges.title: Early warning signals that arrive late
challenges.body: Many institutions run early alert systems, yet alerts often depend on faculty reports or midterm grades that surface problems after students have already disengaged. Behavioral data from learning platforms, advising and campus services could provide earlier insight, but it is rarely integrated or validated against outcomes like persistence and completion.

challenges.title: Belonging that is uneven across students
challenges.body: Students who doubt whether they belong may avoid office hours, hesitate to ask questions and interpret setbacks as signs they should leave. Those doubts are more common among students navigating college without family experience or community models. Belonging initiatives often lack clear behavioral targets and measures, making it hard to know what helps.

challenges.title: Faculty capacity and adoption of new practices
challenges.body: Faculty are asked to adopt active learning, new technologies, inclusive pedagogy and AI policies while maintaining research and service. Mandates without support breed resistance, and good practices spread slowly. Change efforts rarely examine the motivation, ability and prompts faculty need to try something new and sustain it.

challenges.title: Advising and support services that students miss
challenges.body: Tutoring, counseling, career services and financial aid offices can transform a student's experience, but many students who would benefit never use them. Barriers include stigma, uncertainty about eligibility, scheduling friction and simply not knowing a service exists. Outreach often reaches students already inclined to seek help.

challenges.title: Research that does not reach practice
challenges.body: Universities produce knowledge with real public value, yet much of it remains inaccessible to the practitioners, policymakers and communities who could use it. Translation requires understanding audiences, designing usable formats and measuring uptake, skills that are not always rewarded or resourced within academic structures.

how_we_help.title: Student engagement signals and KPIs
how_we_help.body: We integrate learning platform, advising, enrollment and survey data to identify behaviors that predict persistence and success for different student populations. Behavioral Signals Design turns those findings into predictive KPIs and clear hypotheses, so advisors and leaders can act earlier and test which forms of outreach help students re-engage.

how_we_help.title: Learning and belonging design
how_we_help.body: We work with faculty, student affairs and academic leaders to design courses, orientation and support experiences that build competence, autonomy and connection. Grounded in learning research and self-determination theory, interventions target specific moments, such as the first weeks of a term, and are evaluated with appropriate measures.

how_we_help.title: Measurement and survey design
how_we_help.body: Applying psychometrics, we help institutions design or refine measures of engagement, belonging and wellbeing that are reliable and useful for decisions. We also connect survey results with behavioral data, so institutions can see whether what students report aligns with what they do and which interventions affect both.

how_we_help.title: Faculty and leader change support
how_we_help.body: We help academic leaders design change initiatives around faculty reality, identifying small, high-value practices and the support needed to adopt them. Coaching for deans, chairs and senior leaders addresses alignment and communication in shared governance settings, so new practices spread through peer influence rather than mandate alone.

how_we_help.title: Research translation and dissemination
how_we_help.body: We help research centers and faculty translate findings into formats that practitioners and the public can use, from briefs and toolkits to workshops and digital resources. Audience research and testing ensure materials are understood and acted on, and impact measurement tracks whether knowledge actually reaches practice.

industries.impact_lens: Higher education expands opportunity, advances knowledge and prepares people to contribute to their communities. When students disengage and leave, they often carry debt without the credential and lose confidence that education is for them. Behavioral science advances the mission by identifying students who need support earlier, designing environments where more learners feel they belong and helping faculty adopt practices that improve learning. It also helps research institutions share accessible scientific knowledge beyond campus, closing the gap between discovery and the people whose lives it could improve.

faqs.q: How can institutions improve student engagement in higher education?
faqs.a: Start by defining which engagement behaviors predict success for your students, then look for those signals in existing data. Many institutions find that early behaviors, such as consistent learning platform use or connecting with an advisor, matter more than demographic risk factors. Interventions designed around those behaviors and tested carefully tend to be more effective than broad campaigns.

faqs.q: Do you use predictive models to flag students?
faqs.a: We use behavioral analysis to identify signals and patterns, and we are careful about how predictions are applied. Flags should prompt supportive outreach, not labels that limit opportunity. We examine models for bias across student groups, involve advisors and students in designing responses and measure whether outreach actually helps the students it reaches.

faqs.q: Can you support faculty development without adding to faculty workload?
faqs.a: That is a central design goal. We identify small, high-value practices that fit existing routines, provide ready-to-use resources and build peer communities where faculty can learn from each other. Leadership coaching helps chairs and deans protect time for change. The aim is adoption that feels like a relief rather than another obligation.

industries.name: K-12 Education
industries.meta_title: Behavioral Science for K-12 Student Engagement
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science for K-12 student engagement: support attendance, belonging, teacher wellbeing and family partnership with evidence-based, tested design.
industries.summary: Behavioral science for districts, schools and education organizations improving K-12 student engagement, attendance, belonging, teacher wellbeing and family partnership.
industries.lede: K-12 student engagement is built through daily routines, relationships and a sense of belonging. We help districts, schools and education organizations understand the behaviors behind attendance and learning, design practical supports and measure what helps.
context: Schools see behavior every day: who arrives on time, who participates, who completes work and who drifts toward the edges of the classroom. K-12 student engagement shows up in attendance patterns, assignment completion, extracurricular involvement and how students talk about school. Chronic absence and disengagement often begin quietly, with a few missed days or a change in friendships, and become visible as problems only after they affect learning. Districts collect much of this data, but it is spread across student information, learning and survey systems.

Belonging and relationships are foundational. Students who feel known by at least one adult and connected to peers are more likely to attend, participate and seek help. Families are essential partners, yet communication from schools can feel confusing, punitive or one-directional, especially for families who had difficult school experiences or speak languages other than English. Inside schools, teachers manage complex classrooms with limited time, and teacher wellbeing affects both retention and student experience.

Current forces include ongoing recovery in attendance and learning, rising attention to student mental health, staffing shortages, new technology and AI tools in classrooms, and pressure to show results with limited resources. Education leaders need approaches that respect educators' expertise and time. Behavioral science, grounded in learning research and careful measurement, helps schools focus on the few behaviors and moments that matter most and test supports before scaling them, so that limited time and funding go to what helps students.

challenges.title: Chronic absence that builds quietly
