challenges.body: Absences accumulate a day at a time, often for reasons schools do not see: transportation, health, caregiving, anxiety or disconnection. By the time a student is flagged as chronically absent, patterns are entrenched. Communications to families can unintentionally sound punitive, discouraging the partnership that would help students return.

challenges.title: Belonging that some students lack
challenges.body: Students who do not feel they belong are less likely to engage, attend or ask for help. Belonging can be fragile during transitions such as entering middle or high school. Many schools value belonging but lack practical ways to build it consistently and measures that show whether efforts are reaching students who need them.

challenges.title: Teacher time, wellbeing and retention
challenges.body: Teachers face heavy workloads, complex student needs and frequent new initiatives. When new programs arrive without removing old demands, adoption suffers and burnout grows. Teacher turnover disrupts relationships that students depend on, making teacher wellbeing a direct factor in student engagement and learning.

challenges.title: Family communication that misses the mark
challenges.body: Schools send many messages, but families may receive them through the wrong channel, in an unfamiliar language or framed in ways that feel judgmental. Important information gets lost among routine notices. Effective family partnership requires communication designed around how families actually read, decide and act.

challenges.title: Data rich, insight poor
challenges.body: Districts collect attendance, grades, assessments, behavior incidents and survey responses, but integrating them into timely, actionable insight is difficult. Educators receive reports that describe the past rather than signals that suggest where to act next, and data dashboards can add to workload without changing decisions.

how_we_help.title: Attendance and engagement signal analysis
how_we_help.body: We analyze attendance, academic and survey data to identify early patterns that precede chronic absence and disengagement, distinguishing behavioral types such as students with sporadic absences and those withdrawing gradually. Findings become a small set of predictive indicators and practical hypotheses that school teams can act on during the year.

how_we_help.title: Family communication design
how_we_help.body: We redesign attendance notices, school updates and outreach with families, applying behavioral science and plain-language principles. Messages emphasize partnership, clear next steps and the value of each school day, and they are tested through controlled comparisons to learn which approaches increase family response and student attendance.

how_we_help.title: Learning and belonging supports
how_we_help.body: We work with educators to design routines that build connection and competence, such as structured transitions, advisory practices and classroom rituals. Supports are selected for feasibility within existing schedules and grounded in research on motivation and belonging, with measures that show whether students experience a difference.

how_we_help.title: Educator wellbeing and team coaching
how_we_help.body: We coach principals and school teams to reduce initiative overload, strengthen collaboration and build psychological safety for trying new practices. Workflow research identifies the demands that drain teacher time, and leaders learn to protect capacity so that improvement work becomes sustainable rather than another burden.

how_we_help.title: Program evaluation and impact measurement
how_we_help.body: We help districts and education nonprofits design evaluation that fits real school conditions, combining behavioral data, surveys and qualitative insight. Clear logic models and measures show whether programs change the behaviors they target, supporting decisions about what to continue, adjust or stop.

industries.impact_lens: K-12 schools shape children's knowledge, relationships and sense of what is possible. When students disengage or miss school, the effects compound over years and fall unevenly on families with fewer resources. Behavioral science advances education's public good by helping schools notice disengagement earlier, communicate with families as partners and design environments where more students feel they belong. It also protects educators by focusing improvement on the few behaviors that matter. Every intervention should respect students and families and help them do what they already want: learn, grow and thrive.

faqs.q: How does behavioral science improve K-12 student engagement?
faqs.a: It identifies the specific behaviors and moments that shape engagement, such as attendance in the first weeks of school or connection with an adult mentor, and designs supports for them. Instead of broad initiatives, schools focus on a few targeted changes that fit their routines, then measure whether those changes help students attend, participate and learn. Successful approaches can then be shared across schools.

faqs.q: Will this add to teachers' workloads?
faqs.a: We design specifically to avoid that. Interventions are chosen for feasibility within existing schedules, and we often recommend removing or simplifying tasks alongside any new practice. Teachers and school leaders participate in design, and we test changes at small scale so that only approaches that prove useful are expanded across classrooms or schools.

faqs.q: Do you work with education nonprofits and edtech organizations?
faqs.a: Yes. Education nonprofits and edtech organizations face related questions about student engagement, family communication, product adoption and evidence of impact. We apply the same behavioral methods, adapting them to each organization's role in the education system and to the needs of the schools and families it serves, with evaluation designed in from the start.

industries.name: Associations & Nonprofits
industries.meta_title: Association Member Engagement and Behavioral Science
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science for association member engagement: clarify member value, improve renewals, design public education campaigns and measure impact.
industries.summary: Behavioral science for associations and nonprofits strengthening association member engagement, clarifying member value, running public education campaigns and measuring mission impact.
industries.lede: Association member engagement depends on whether members feel the organization makes a real difference in their work and lives. We help associations and nonprofits understand member behavior, communicate value clearly and design public education that changes behavior.
context: Associations and nonprofits exist to serve members, professions and communities, yet many face a familiar tension. Members join for credentials, events, advocacy or community, then engage with only a small part of what the organization offers. Renewal becomes a habit for some and a question for others. Association member engagement is often measured through event attendance or email opens, which say little about whether members perceive enough value to stay, volunteer or recommend the organization to peers.

Inside these organizations, staff and volunteer leaders work with limited resources, complex governance and boards that may hold different views about priorities. Data lives in association management systems, learning platforms, event tools and email platforms that rarely connect with one another. Decisions about programs and pricing are often made on long-held assumptions about what members want. Generational shifts in how professionals seek community and learning challenge models built for earlier career patterns.

Many associations and nonprofits also run public education campaigns: encouraging health screenings, promoting safety practices or helping the public understand a profession's role. These campaigns are behavior change efforts, yet they are frequently designed around awareness alone. Current forces, including fragmented media, declining trust in institutions and misinformation, make it harder to reach audiences. Behavioral science helps organizations clarify member value, design campaigns that prompt action and measure impact credibly.

challenges.title: Member value that is unclear
challenges.body: Members often cannot articulate what they gain from membership beyond a single benefit. When the value proposition is diffuse, renewal depends on inertia, and price increases or budget pressures prompt cancellations. Organizations need to know which experiences actually create perceived value for different types of members.

challenges.title: Engagement measured by activity, not meaning
challenges.body: Open rates, logins and attendance are easy to count but may not predict renewal, volunteering or advocacy. Some highly valuable members engage rarely but deeply, while others participate often without strong commitment. Without behavior-based KPIs, associations invest in programs that look busy rather than those that build loyalty.

challenges.title: Public campaigns that stop at awareness
challenges.body: Public education efforts often aim to raise awareness, assuming action will follow. People may know a screening is recommended or a practice is safer and still not act. Campaigns that ignore ability, timing and prompts rarely change behavior, and success is hard to measure beyond reach and impressions.

challenges.title: Volunteer leaders and governance dynamics
challenges.body: Boards and committees bring expertise and commitment, but rotating leadership, differing priorities and limited time can slow decisions. Staff leaders must align volunteers around strategy without authority over them. Change initiatives stall when governance conversations rely on opinion instead of shared evidence about member behavior.

challenges.title: Demonstrating mission impact
challenges.body: Funders, members and boards increasingly ask nonprofits and associations to show the difference they make. Many organizations track outputs, such as programs delivered or people reached, rather than changes in behavior or outcomes. Building credible impact measurement requires clear logic, practical measures and analysis that resource-constrained teams can sustain.

how_we_help.title: Member value and engagement research
how_we_help.body: We interview and survey members, lapsed members and prospects to understand which experiences create value for different member types. Combined with behavioral analysis of membership data, the research shows where value is perceived and where it is assumed, giving leaders evidence for decisions about programs, pricing and communications.

how_we_help.title: Behavior-based member KPIs
how_we_help.body: We identify the member behaviors that predict renewal, volunteering and advocacy, such as early participation in a community or use of a professional resource. These become predictive KPIs and dashboard views that staff and boards can use to spot risk and opportunity well before the renewal cycle.

how_we_help.title: Public education campaign design
how_we_help.body: We design public awareness and education campaigns as behavior change programs, defining the target action, the barriers audiences face and the prompts that could help. Messages and channels are tested with representative audiences, and campaigns are evaluated against the behaviors they aim to change rather than reach alone.

how_we_help.title: Board and leadership alignment
how_we_help.body: We facilitate alignment among staff leadership, boards and committees using shared data about member behavior and mission outcomes. Structured conversations and coaching help leaders agree on priorities, clarify roles and make decisions with evidence, reducing the friction that slows change in volunteer-led organizations.

how_we_help.title: Impact measurement and evaluation
how_we_help.body: We help organizations build practical impact measurement, including logic models, behavioral and outcome indicators and data collection that fits staff capacity. Evaluation findings support funder reporting, board decisions and program improvement, and they help organizations communicate impact honestly without overstating results.

industries.impact_lens: Associations and nonprofits advance professions, protect public health and safety, share knowledge and strengthen communities. Their impact depends on engaged members and on public audiences who take recommended actions. Behavioral science advances that social good by clarifying what members truly value, designing campaigns that move people from awareness to action and measuring outcomes credibly. It helps mission-driven organizations spend limited resources where they make the most difference, and it supports ethical persuasion that respects audiences while encouraging the behaviors that protect health, safety and wellbeing.

faqs.q: How can associations improve member engagement and renewal?
faqs.a: Start by understanding which experiences create real value for different member types, then identify the early behaviors that predict renewal. Association member engagement improves when organizations design around those behaviors, for example by helping new members reach a valuable resource or community quickly, and when communications emphasize the value members have actually experienced.

faqs.q: What makes a public education campaign change behavior?
faqs.a: Effective campaigns define a specific action, understand what prevents the audience from taking it and design prompts and supports that make the action easier at the right moment. Awareness is often necessary but rarely sufficient. Testing messages with representative audiences and measuring behavior, not just reach, shows whether a campaign is working.

faqs.q: Can small nonprofits afford behavioral science work?
faqs.a: Engagements can be scoped to fit. Many organizations begin with a focused question, such as improving one renewal pathway or testing one campaign message, using data they already have. Workshops and training also help staff apply behavioral principles independently. The aim is to build lasting capability, not dependence on outside advisors.

industries.name: Technology & SaaS
industries.meta_title: SaaS User Activation and Product Adoption Design
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science for SaaS user activation and adoption: find the behaviors that predict retention, redesign onboarding and test what drives expansion.
industries.summary: Behavioral science for technology and SaaS companies improving user activation, feature adoption, retention and the team behaviors that sustain product-led growth.
industries.lede: SaaS user activation is where retention is won or lost. We help technology companies identify the behaviors that predict lasting value, design onboarding and adoption around them and build teams that run disciplined experiments.
context: Software companies collect more behavioral data than almost any other industry, yet many still struggle to explain why some accounts thrive and others churn. Product analytics show clicks and sessions, but SaaS user activation depends on whether users reach a meaningful outcome early enough to form a habit. Teams often define activation by convenience, such as completing setup, rather than by the behaviors that actually predict retention and expansion. The result is onboarding optimized for the wrong moment.

Adoption is also an organizational behavior. In business software, an individual champion may love a product while colleagues ignore it, and renewal depends on whether usage spreads across teams. Administrators, end users and economic buyers have different motivations and constraints. Inside the company, product, design, customer success, sales and marketing each hold part of the adoption story and are measured on different numbers, which makes it difficult to agree on what to fix first.

Current forces sharpen these questions. AI features are being added rapidly, but users adopt them only when they trust the output and understand where it fits their work. Buyers scrutinize spend and expect clear value. Product-led and sales-led motions blend, raising questions about handoffs. Growing companies also face leadership challenges as teams scale. Behavioral science offers a disciplined way to connect product data, user research and experimentation around the behaviors that drive durable growth.

challenges.title: Activation defined by setup, not value
challenges.body: Many teams count a user as activated after completing onboarding steps. Those steps may have little to do with the value that keeps customers. Without validating activation against retention, companies optimize flows that look successful while users leave before experiencing what the product is actually good at.

challenges.title: Features shipped but not adopted
challenges.body: Roadmaps deliver new features, including AI capabilities, that only a small share of users discover or use repeatedly. Announcements and tooltips rarely change established workflows. Adoption depends on relevance, timing and trust, and teams often lack research into how users decide whether a new feature is worth the effort.

challenges.title: Account adoption beyond the champion
challenges.body: In business software, a single enthusiastic user does not guarantee renewal. Value must spread to teams and become embedded in workflows. Customer success teams may see usage concentrated in a few people without knowing which behaviors signal healthy account adoption or what would help it expand.

challenges.title: Experiments without behavioral hypotheses
challenges.body: Many SaaS companies run A/B tests, but tests often vary button colors or copy without a clear theory of behavior. Results are inconclusive or fail to generalize. Experimentation becomes more valuable when hypotheses are grounded in behavioral models and connected to predictive KPIs that matter for retention.

challenges.title: Scaling teams and decision quality
challenges.body: Rapid growth adds people, layers and handoffs faster than leadership practices mature. Product and go-to-market teams may disagree about priorities, and decisions slow or become political. Leaders who were effective at small scale must learn new ways to align teams, delegate and decide under pressure.

how_we_help.title: Activation and conversion analytics
how_we_help.body: We analyze product event data to find the early behaviors that predict retention and expansion, then define activation around them. Conversion behavior analytics identifies where users stall on the path to those behaviors, and behavioral segmentation shows which user types need different paths. The outcome is a validated activation metric and a prioritized list of hypotheses.

how_we_help.title: Onboarding and activation design
how_we_help.body: We redesign onboarding around the first meaningful outcome rather than the full setup checklist. Approaches include progressive setup, templates that deliver early value and prompts timed to real work. Usability testing with representative users catches confusion early, and experiments confirm which changes improve activation and early retention.

how_we_help.title: Feature and AI adoption strategy
how_we_help.body: We research how users decide whether to adopt new capabilities, including AI features where trust and transparency matter. Adoption strategies focus on relevance, ease of first use and in-context prompts. We also help teams set responsible design standards so AI features support user judgment rather than replacing it without explanation.

how_we_help.title: Experimentation program design
how_we_help.body: We help product and growth teams build experimentation programs grounded in behavioral hypotheses, sound statistical design and predictive KPIs. That includes prioritization frameworks, test documentation and review routines that turn individual tests into cumulative learning about how customers behave and what they value.

how_we_help.title: Leadership for scaling teams
how_we_help.body: We coach founders and executives through the leadership transitions that come with growth, from delegating decisions to aligning product and go-to-market teams. Team coaching builds the trust and decision routines that let scaling organizations move quickly without losing clarity about priorities.

industries.impact_lens: Software increasingly shapes how people work, learn, communicate and access services. When technology is hard to adopt, it wastes time, frustrates users and widens gaps between those who can navigate complexity and those who cannot. Behavioral science advances the social good in technology by designing products around real human attention and ability, encouraging persuasive design that serves users' own goals and helping teams adopt AI responsibly. Companies that measure activation by genuine value create products people choose to keep using, which is better for users and for sustainable growth.

faqs.q: How do you define SaaS user activation?
faqs.a: We define activation by the early behaviors that statistically predict retention and expansion for your product, not by setup completion alone. That requires analyzing historical cohorts, testing candidate definitions and confirming them with user research. A good activation metric is specific, observable early and clearly connected to the value customers pay for.

faqs.q: How is this different from what our product analytics team does?
faqs.a: We complement internal analytics rather than replace it. Our contribution is a behavioral science lens: theories about why users act as they do, qualitative research to explain patterns, measurement design and experiments built around clear hypotheses. We often work alongside product analysts to strengthen the link between data, design and decisions.

faqs.q: Can you help with AI feature adoption?
faqs.a: Yes. AI features raise distinctive adoption questions around trust, explainability and fit with existing workflows. We research how users evaluate AI output, design onboarding and prompts that build appropriate trust and help teams define standards for responsible use. Adoption is measured by sustained, valuable use rather than first trials or one-time experiments.

industries.name: Retail & Consumer Brands
industries.meta_title: Consumer Behavior Research for Retail and Brands
industries.meta_description: Consumer behavior research for retail and consumer brands: find the conversion moments that matter, test messaging and build loyalty customers choose.
industries.summary: Behavioral science and consumer behavior research for retailers and consumer brands improving conversion, loyalty, brand messaging and the frontline experiences that shape repeat purchase.
industries.lede: Consumer behavior research is most useful when it explains what people actually do, not only what they say. We help retailers and consumer brands find the moments that drive purchase and loyalty, test messaging and design experiences customers return to.
context: Retailers and consumer brands have access to vast amounts of data: point-of-sale transactions, ecommerce behavior, loyalty programs, app usage, reviews and survey results. Yet many still rely on demographic personas and stated preferences that explain little about why customers choose, switch or return. What shoppers say in surveys often differs from what they do at the shelf or in the cart, where habit, context, emotion and small frictions decide outcomes. Consumer behavior research grounded in behavioral science closes that gap.

Inside these organizations, merchandising, marketing, ecommerce, store operations and customer service each own part of the customer experience. Store associates shape impressions in ways that rarely appear in dashboards, and their engagement affects customer loyalty directly. Data sits in separate platforms, and teams often run disconnected tests that are difficult to compare. Decisions about promotions, assortment and messaging may rest on long-standing assumptions that have never been tested against behavior.

Current forces add complexity. Shoppers move fluidly between stores, apps, marketplaces and social channels. Price sensitivity and private label competition test brand loyalty. Personalization and AI-generated recommendations raise both opportunities and privacy concerns. Consumers expect brands to be honest about sustainability and value. Retailers and brands that understand the behavioral drivers of choice, and that use persuasion responsibly, are better placed to earn repeat purchase rather than buying it with discounts.

challenges.title: Personas that do not predict behavior
challenges.body: Demographic personas are easy to communicate but often fail to explain purchase patterns. Two customers with the same profile may shop entirely differently. Without behavioral segments based on how people actually buy, brands misallocate marketing spend and design experiences for an average customer who does not exist.

challenges.title: Conversion lost to small frictions
challenges.body: In both stores and digital channels, purchases are lost to minor obstacles: unclear pricing, crowded choices, slow checkout or uncertainty about returns. These frictions are hard to see in aggregate reports. Brands need methods that locate the specific conversion points where intention turns into abandonment.

challenges.title: Loyalty programs that reward discounts
challenges.body: Many loyalty programs train customers to wait for promotions rather than building genuine preference. Points and offers drive short-term activity but may erode margin and brand meaning. The behavioral question is what creates lasting attachment, such as convenience, recognition or identity, and how to measure it.

challenges.title: Messaging tested by opinion
challenges.body: Creative and messaging decisions are frequently made by internal preference or small focus groups. Messages that sound compelling to teams may not change consumer behavior. Without structured research and experimentation, brands risk investing in campaigns that win approval internally but have little effect on choice.

challenges.title: Frontline experience left unmeasured
challenges.body: Store associates and service teams influence whether customers feel welcomed, helped and confident. Their behavior is rarely measured in ways that connect to customer outcomes, and engagement programs for frontline staff are often generic. The link between employee experience and customer loyalty remains an untested assumption.

how_we_help.title: Behavioral segmentation
how_we_help.body: We analyze transaction, loyalty and digital data to define behavioral types: groups of customers who share patterns of purchase, channel use and response to promotion. These segments guide targeting, assortment and experience design more effectively than demographic personas, and each comes with hypotheses about what would increase its value.

how_we_help.title: Conversion behavior analytics
how_we_help.body: We trace the path to purchase across store and digital channels to find the moments where intention is lost. Combining analytics with observation and usability research shows why customers abandon, not only where. The result is a prioritized set of design changes and experiments targeting the highest-value conversion points.

how_we_help.title: Brand messaging research
how_we_help.body: We test messaging, claims and creative concepts with representative consumers using structured research and, where possible, in-market experiments. Behavioral science informs how messages are framed and how results are interpreted, helping brands choose communication that changes behavior and avoids overstated or misleading appeals.

how_we_help.title: Retention and loyalty strategy
how_we_help.body: We help brands design loyalty around the behaviors and motivations that create genuine preference rather than discount dependence. That may include recognition, convenience, personalization with clear consent and community. Pilots measure repeat purchase and margin together, so loyalty investment is judged by durable value.

how_we_help.title: Customer experience research
how_we_help.body: We combine shopper interviews, in-store observation and associate research to understand how experiences feel on the ground. Findings connect frontline behavior with customer outcomes and inform service design, training and coaching for store leaders, so improvements reflect what customers and associates actually experience.

industries.impact_lens: Retail and consumer brands shape everyday choices about food, health, household budgets and sustainability. Behavioral science can make those choices easier and more aligned with what people value, or it can exploit attention and impulse. We advocate the former: clear information, honest messaging, fair loyalty programs and personalization that respects privacy. Designing for informed choice builds trust that lasts longer than any promotion. It also recognizes frontline associates as central to customer experience, supporting workplaces where employees can do good work and customers feel genuinely served.

faqs.q: How is consumer behavior research different from traditional market research?
faqs.a: Traditional market research often relies on what consumers say about their preferences and intentions. Consumer behavior research grounded in behavioral science also examines what people actually do, using transaction data, observation and experiments. Combining stated and observed behavior gives a more accurate picture of what drives choice and loyalty, and of which changes are worth testing first.

faqs.q: Can you work with both store and ecommerce data?
faqs.a: Yes. Customers move across channels, so we integrate store transactions, ecommerce events, app usage and loyalty data where possible. Where data cannot be linked directly, we use research and careful analysis to understand cross-channel behavior. The goal is to see the customer journey as customers experience it, not as separate channel reports.

faqs.q: How do you keep behavioral design ethical in retail?
faqs.a: We avoid tactics that rely on manufactured urgency, hidden costs or confusing choices. Our approach focuses on reducing genuine friction, clarifying value and helping customers make decisions they will be satisfied with later. We believe trust is a durable commercial asset, and we test interventions for customer satisfaction as well as conversion.

industries.name: Professional & Knowledge Services
industries.meta_title: Behavioral Science for Professional Services Firms
industries.meta_description: Behavioral science for professional services firms: strengthen client relationships, cross-selling, partner leadership and the adoption of new tools and AI.
industries.summary: Behavioral science and leadership coaching for professional services firms improving client relationships, cross-selling, partner leadership, knowledge sharing and responsible AI adoption.
industries.lede: Professional services firms sell expertise, judgment and trust, all of which are expressed through behavior. We help consulting, accounting, legal, engineering and advisory firms strengthen client relationships, align partners and adopt new ways of working.
context: In professional services firms, the product is people. Client value depends on how professionals listen, advise, collaborate and deliver, and growth depends on whether clients trust the firm enough to bring it more of their work. Yet firms often manage these behaviors indirectly, through utilization, billing and revenue targets. Those measures matter, but they lag. They reveal problems with client relationships or team effectiveness long after the behaviors that caused them have taken hold.

Partnership structures create distinctive people problems. Partners are owners, producers and leaders at once, with significant autonomy and strong personal relationships with clients. Collaboration across practices can feel risky, and leadership decisions often require consensus among peers. Talented professionals are promoted for technical excellence, then asked to lead teams and develop people without preparation. Knowledge sits with individuals, and firms struggle to share it in ways that improve quality across the organization.

Current forces are changing the work itself. AI tools are automating research, drafting and analysis, raising questions about pricing, training of junior staff and the nature of professional judgment. Clients expect integrated advice across disciplines. Talent expectations around flexibility and development continue to shift. Professional services firms that understand the behaviors behind client trust, collaboration and adoption are better prepared to adapt without losing the culture that made them successful.

challenges.title: Client relationships held by individuals
challenges.body: Many client relationships depend on one or two partners. When those partners retire or move, relationships are at risk. Firms want institutional relationships, but professionals may hesitate to introduce colleagues or share client insight. The behaviors that build firm-level trust are rarely defined or developed deliberately.

challenges.title: Cross-practice collaboration that stalls
challenges.body: Clients could benefit from expertise across practices, yet referrals between partners remain limited. Concerns about quality, credit and client experience outweigh incentives. Without understanding the behavioral barriers to referral, firms invest in account programs and technology that leave underlying habits unchanged.

challenges.title: Leaders promoted for technical excellence
challenges.body: Professionals often reach leadership roles because they are excellent practitioners. Leading teams, giving feedback and managing conflict require different skills that are rarely taught. Without development, new leaders default to doing the work themselves, limiting team growth and contributing to burnout across levels.

challenges.title: AI adoption and professional judgment
challenges.body: AI tools promise efficiency in research, drafting and analysis, but adoption is uneven and raises concerns about quality, confidentiality and the development of junior professionals. Firms need to decide where AI supports judgment, where human review is essential and how to bring skeptical professionals along.

challenges.title: Feedback measured too slowly
challenges.body: Client satisfaction surveys and annual reviews provide feedback months after the interactions that shaped them. Firms lack timely signals about client sentiment, team health and engagement. Leaders make decisions about staffing, pricing and investment with lagging information and untested assumptions.

how_we_help.title: Cross-sell and client relationship design
how_we_help.body: We study how client relationships and referrals actually develop in your firm, through partner interviews and analysis of client and engagement data. We then design processes for client teams, introductions and account planning that build trust between practices and make collaboration feel safe and valuable for partners and clients.

how_we_help.title: Executive coaching for partners
how_we_help.body: We coach partners and practice leaders on the behaviors that matter in their roles: developing teams, leading peers without formal authority, managing difficult client conversations and making decisions under pressure. Coaching is confidential, goal-directed and grounded in behavioral science and clinical psychology.

how_we_help.title: Leadership development for new leaders
how_we_help.body: We design leadership programs for professionals moving into management, focused on feedback, delegation, psychological safety and team performance. Programs combine practical skills with coaching and peer learning, and they define observable behaviors so firms can see whether development is taking hold.

how_we_help.title: Responsible AI adoption
how_we_help.body: We help firms adopt AI tools in ways that protect quality, confidentiality and professional development. That includes understanding how professionals actually use AI, designing workflows where human judgment is clearly placed and building adoption plans that address skepticism with evidence rather than mandates.

how_we_help.title: People analytics and predictive measures
how_we_help.body: We help firms build timely measures of client sentiment, team health and engagement, drawing on surveys, operational data and psychometric design. These predictive KPIs give leaders earlier insight than annual reviews and highlight where coaching, staffing or process changes are needed.

industries.impact_lens: Professional services firms help organizations make sound decisions, comply with laws, manage risk and build infrastructure, so the quality of their judgment affects many people beyond their direct clients. Behavioral science supports that public value by strengthening how professionals collaborate, lead and learn, and by helping firms adopt AI responsibly without eroding the expertise future professionals need. Healthier partnership cultures reduce burnout, improve retention and produce better advice. When firms understand the behaviors behind trust, they serve clients more completely and contribute to a more capable professional workforce.

faqs.q: What types of professional services firms do you work with?
faqs.a: We work with consulting, accounting, legal, engineering, architecture, advisory and other knowledge-based firms. The common thread is that value depends on expertise, judgment and relationships. We adapt our approach to each firm's partnership structure, client base and culture, recognizing that professional norms, regulation and client expectations vary across disciplines and markets.

faqs.q: How do you help partners collaborate across practices?
faqs.a: We start by understanding the specific concerns that limit referrals, such as client experience, credit and familiarity with colleagues. We then design processes, routines and leadership practices that address those concerns directly and track leading behaviors, like joint client meetings, that predict collaborative growth. Incentives are part of the picture but rarely the whole answer.

faqs.q: Is executive coaching confidential for partners?
faqs.a: Yes. Coaching conversations are confidential, and goals are agreed with the individual partner. When a firm sponsors coaching, we agree in advance what will be shared, typically progress on development goals rather than conversation content. That clarity builds the trust coaching requires while giving the firm appropriate visibility into whether the investment is helping.

industries.name: Private Equity & Portfolio Companies
industries.meta_title: Behavioral Due Diligence for Private Equity
industries.meta_description: Behavioral due diligence for private equity: read customer signals, assess management teams and drive portfolio value creation with predictive KPIs.
industries.summary: Behavioral due diligence, management team assessment and value creation support for private equity investors and their portfolio companies, from deal evaluation through exit.
industries.lede: Behavioral due diligence gives private equity investors evidence about what customers and leaders actually do, not only what they report. We read customer and commercial signals before a deal, assess management teams and help portfolio companies create value.
context: Private equity investors evaluate businesses under time pressure and with incomplete information. Financial diligence shows what happened. Customer and commercial diligence should explain why, and whether it will continue. Behavioral due diligence examines how customers actually buy, renew, expand and churn, using transaction, product and contract data alongside interviews. It distinguishes durable loyalty from inertia and reveals whether growth depends on a few behaviors that are fragile or on habits that are well established.

The management team is often the largest variable in an investment thesis. Investors want to know how leaders make decisions under pressure, whether the team can scale and how it will respond to the demands of a new ownership model. Traditional assessments rely on interviews and references, which can miss the behavioral patterns that matter. Structured management team assessment, grounded in psychometrics and observation, gives deal teams clearer evidence and gives leaders a fair, development-oriented starting point.

After close, value creation plans set ambitious goals for revenue growth, margin improvement and operational change. Many plans depend on people doing things differently: sales teams adopting new processes, customers moving to new products and leaders aligning across functions. Data across portfolio companies is often inconsistent, making progress hard to see. Investors and operating partners who treat these as behavioral challenges, with predictive KPIs and tested interventions, can track value creation earlier and course-correct before results slip.

challenges.title: Customer diligence built on surveys alone
challenges.body: Diligence timelines often lead to customer surveys and reference calls that describe stated satisfaction. Satisfied customers can still churn, and dissatisfied customers may stay because switching is hard. Without analysis of actual behavior, such as usage trends, renewal patterns and purchase concentration, investors may misread the durability of revenue.

challenges.title: Management risk that is hard to see
challenges.body: Deal teams form views of leaders through limited meetings in which executives present their best selves. Behavioral patterns under pressure, team dynamics and gaps in capability are difficult to assess in that setting. Misjudging management fit is costly, and discovering it after close slows value creation and strains relationships.

challenges.title: Value creation plans that depend on behavior change
challenges.body: Plans assume price increases will hold, cross-sell will grow and new systems will be adopted. Each assumption depends on how customers, employees and leaders behave. When plans treat these as operational tasks rather than behavioral challenges, adoption lags and expected value arrives late or not at all.

challenges.title: Lagging, inconsistent portfolio metrics
challenges.body: Portfolio companies often report different metrics, defined in different ways, from systems of varying quality. Operating partners see financial results after the quarter closes without leading indicators of customer health or team performance. Comparing companies and identifying where to intervene is difficult.

challenges.title: Leadership strain during transformation
challenges.body: Ownership transitions bring new expectations, reporting demands and pace. Founders and long-tenured executives may struggle to adapt, and leadership teams may fragment under pressure. Without support, turnover in key roles can disrupt the plan, while the remaining leaders carry heavier loads with limited capacity for strategic work.

how_we_help.title: Customer and commercial due diligence
how_we_help.body: We analyze transaction, product usage, contract and CRM data alongside targeted customer interviews to assess how customers actually behave. Behavioral due diligence identifies the conversion points and behavioral types behind revenue, distinguishes loyalty from inertia and surfaces risks and upside that financial diligence alone may miss, within deal timelines.

how_we_help.title: Management team assessment
how_we_help.body: We assess leadership teams using structured interviews, validated psychometric instruments and behavioral observation. Assessments focus on decision-making under pressure, team dynamics and readiness for the value creation plan. Findings inform investment decisions and become a fair, development-oriented foundation for leaders after close.

how_we_help.title: Portfolio value creation
how_we_help.body: We help operating partners and portfolio leaders identify the customer and employee behaviors each value creation lever depends on, then design and test interventions to change them. Examples include sales process redesign, product adoption and retention programs. Progress is measured with behavior-based KPIs that move before financial results.

how_we_help.title: Predictive portfolio KPIs
how_we_help.body: We define a consistent set of predictive, behavior-based KPIs across portfolio companies, adapted to each business model. Dashboards give investors and operating teams earlier visibility into customer health, adoption and team performance, making it easier to compare companies and focus support where it matters most.

how_we_help.title: Leadership coaching through the hold period
how_we_help.body: We coach portfolio CEOs and leadership teams through ownership transitions and transformation, focusing on alignment, decision-making under pressure and team performance. Coaching builds the leadership capacity a value creation plan requires and helps founders and executives adapt to new expectations while protecting what made the business successful.

industries.impact_lens: Private equity ownership affects employees, customers and communities, not only investors. Behavioral science contributes to better outcomes for all of them by grounding investment decisions in evidence about real customer value, assessing leaders fairly and supporting them through change. Value creation that depends on understanding customers and developing people tends to be more durable than value extracted through short-term cost cutting. When investors measure the behaviors behind performance, they can build companies that serve customers better, support employees through transitions and leave stronger organizations behind at exit.

faqs.q: What is behavioral due diligence?
faqs.a: Behavioral due diligence examines how a target company's customers and leaders actually behave, using transaction, product and contract data, interviews and structured assessment. It complements financial and traditional commercial diligence by explaining the behaviors behind revenue and leadership performance, helping investors judge whether results are durable and where value creation opportunities lie.

faqs.q: Can this work within a typical deal timeline?
faqs.a: Yes. We scope diligence to the time and data available, focusing on the questions most material to the investment thesis. Where full data access is limited, we prioritize the analyses and interviews that provide the clearest signal. Findings are delivered in a format deal teams can use directly in investment committee discussions.

faqs.q: How is management team assessment handled with leaders?
faqs.a: Assessment is conducted transparently and respectfully, with clear explanation of purpose and process. We use validated instruments and structured methods to reduce bias. After close, findings are typically shared with leaders as a development foundation, so the assessment supports their success rather than serving only as an evaluation for the deal team.
